n: In this lecture we consider transport trauma. Transport trauma is the set of injuries received from the parts of a moving vehicle and from a fall from it; auto trauma is one such type. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1.2 million people die in road traffic accidents every year, and more than 50 million are injured. Transport trauma accounts for 60-65 per cent of deaths from mechanical injury, and auto trauma for more than 90 per cent of examinations. For this reason, since the 1960s transport trauma has been singled out as a separate part of forensic medicine. The reason is the mechanism of injury and the particular nature of the examination.

We turn to the key questions on the topic. The questions cover the classification of blunt objects, the difference between compression and inertial trauma, the mechanisms of action, and the significance of abrasions and bruises. Questions are also asked about the properties of wounds and the permanent deformation of bones. Also listed as questions are the injuries formed in a fall from a height and onto a flat surface. That is, this list shows what we should rely on in mastering the topic.

We consider the general features of sawing wounds. When struck with a saw, many small stab or stab-incised wounds are formed, corresponding to the size of the teeth and arranged in a track. If the blow is strong, a broken linear wound arises, at the base of which tissue bridges are visible between the wound walls. The edges of a wound from a circular saw are uneven, toothed and sometimes with small flaps. The sawn surface of bone is relatively smooth, with arc-shaped marks. Remember: inside the wound, at its edges and around it there are small particles of soft tissue and bone sawdust. This is an important feature of a sawing wound.

t: Marks of circular and blade saws
n: Now we compare the marks of circular and blade saws. The kerf is wider than the thickness of the saw blade. When struck with the saw, a row of small stab or stab-incised wounds is formed, corresponding to the size of the teeth. Particles of soft tissue and bone sawdust are found inside and around the wound. In the circular saw the movement is rotary; the edges are uneven, toothed, with small flaps, and relatively smooth arc-shaped marks remain on the bone. In the blade saw the movement is back and forth; the wound is linear, finely toothed, with abrasion, and parallel ridges and grooves are visible on the bone.

Let us look at a case analysis. The wound is linear, its edges are finely toothed and uneven, and there are signs of abrasion; superficial cuts and scratches were found at the ends. On the sawn surface of the bone, parallel ridges and grooves corresponding to the saw blade were found. The question is: which saw was used, circular or blade? The answer must be justified by the features. Attention, there is a risk of error here: arc-shaped marks are characteristic of a circular saw, and parallel grooves of a blade saw.

t: Concept and prevalence of transport trauma
n: We move on to the concept and prevalence of transport trauma. Transport trauma is the set of injuries received from the external and internal parts of a moving vehicle and from a fall from it. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1.2 million people die in road traffic accidents every year, and more than 50 million are injured. According to World Bank estimates, material damage amounts to 1.5-2.0 per cent of the gross domestic product, that is, GDP, of all countries. This means that the problem is of significance not only medically but also economically.

t: Share of transport trauma in examination
n: We look at the share of transport trauma in examination. Transport trauma accounts for 60-65 per cent of deaths from mechanical injury. In the examination of living persons, transport trauma makes up 20-25 per cent of mechanical injuries. The share of auto trauma exceeds 90 per cent. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1.2 million people die every year and more than 50 million are injured. That is, transport trauma is among the mechanical injuries most frequently encountered in expert practice.

We speak about the types of transport trauma. Transport trauma is the set of injuries received from the parts of a vehicle and from a fall from it. The diagram of types shows automobile, motorcycle and bicycle, tractor and rail, aviation and water transport. A separate group is combined trauma: it arises when different vehicles collide, for example in a collision of a motorcycle with a car. Auto trauma, in turn, is the most frequently encountered type of transport trauma.

We consider the question of preserving clothing and prevention. The physician must fully examine and describe the injury, and also pay attention to the victim's clothing and footwear. The clothing and footwear may bear signs of injury and contamination that are important for investigating the incident, so they must be removed carefully. If necessary, the clothing is dried under room conditions, placed in paper packaging and handed over to law enforcement officers. Analysis of examination materials makes it possible to give proposals and recommendations for measures aimed at reducing transport injury.

Case analysis. A child struck by a car on the road is brought to hospital. The physician fully examines the injuries and describes them in detail. Attention is also paid to the child's clothing and footwear, since they may bear signs of injury and contamination. The clothing is removed as carefully as possible, dried indoors if necessary, placed in paper packaging and handed over to the law enforcement bodies. Question: why must the clothing and footwear not be thrown away, and what information for the examination may be preserved on them?

We consolidate knowledge with quick questions. First question: what is transport trauma? Answer: the set of injuries received from the external and internal parts of a moving vehicle and from a fall from it. Second question: how many people die each year according to the World Health Organization? Answer: more than 1.2 million, and more than 50 million are injured. Third question: what share of deaths from mechanical injury is due to transport trauma? Answer: 60-65 per cent; in living persons, 20-25 per cent of mechanical injuries. Fourth question: which type is the leading one? Answer: automobile trauma, more than 90 per cent of examinations.

We study auto trauma and Matyshev's classification. Auto trauma is the most frequently encountered type of transport trauma; it is the set of injuries received from the external and internal parts of a car and from a fall from it. According to the 1968 classification of Matyshev and co-authors, six types of auto trauma are distinguished. These are collision, running over by a wheel, injury inside the car, falling out of the car, that is, a fall, compression between the car and another object, and the combined type. In the combined type, two or more types occur together.

t: The four groups of injuries in auto trauma
n: We consider the four groups of injuries in auto trauma. By diagnostic significance, injuries are conventionally divided into four groups: specific, characteristic, non-characteristic and imitative. A specific injury reflects the shape and pattern of a part of the car, and from it the type, and sometimes the particular car, is determined. A characteristic injury corresponds to a certain type or phase. A non-characteristic injury has neither specific nor characteristic features. An imitative injury resembles an injury in another incident. The grouping helps to determine the mechanism of injury, the type of auto trauma and sometimes its phase, and is also of practical importance in distinguishing auto trauma from injuries in another incident.

We consider specific and characteristic injuries. A specific, that is, contact, injury is formed under the action of a particular part of the car, for example a headlamp, a decorative front part or a tyre tread, and its shape corresponds to that part. Characteristic injuries include the bumper injury, sliding and dragging marks, multiple rib fractures and blood pockets. A bumper injury is usually a transverse abrasion, bruise or wound. A bumper fracture is triangular in shape, with its base on the side of the primary impact. A whiplash fracture of the cervical vertebrae and a compression fracture of the vertebral bodies are also among the characteristic injuries.

We distinguish non-characteristic and imitative injuries. Non-characteristic injuries lack specific and characteristic features, so no conclusion about auto trauma can be drawn from them. This group mainly includes abrasions, bruises and some wounds on the body. In an imitative injury, fragments of the windscreen resemble an incised or stab-incised wound, and protruding bolts resemble a stab wound. Attention: an imitative injury resembles injuries in other incidents, so it can be misleading.

Case analysis: groups of injuries. In a pedestrian, a mark resembling the shape of a headlamp, multiple rib fractures and an incised wound were found. Question: to which of the four groups does each injury belong, and what does it show about auto trauma? Look at the table: the mark reproducing the shape of the headlamp is specific; the bumper injury and multiple rib fractures are characteristic; ordinary abrasions and bruises are non-characteristic; the incised wound from windscreen fragments is imitative. Remember: an injury from glass fragments resembles an incised wound but is not characteristic of auto trauma. The concepts of specific and characteristic are not identical.

t: Collision with a pedestrian: four phases
n: We consider the four phases of a collision with a pedestrian. In a collision with the front of a car, four phases are distinguished. The first is impact by the parts, that is, the primary action. The second is falling onto the car; with a lorry this phase is absent. The third is being thrown and falling to the ground. The fourth is sliding along the ground, in which parallel abrasions are formed. In small children the second phase is not observed, because the impact falls above the centre of gravity. At low speed the fourth phase may be absent.

We dwell on bumper injuries. Under the action of the bumper, a transversely placed abrasion, bruise or wound is usually formed. In a collision with a passenger car the bones of the leg are broken, and with a lorry the femora; this depends on the height of the bumper and the speed. A bumper fracture is usually triangular, with its base on the side of the primary impact. If the bumper is thin and the speed is greater than 55-60 km/h, a ring-shaped fracture may arise in the bones.

We consider the map of injuries by phase. In the first phase, abrasions and bruises resembling the shape of the headlamp and bumper are formed, that is, contact injuries; this is the zone of primary action and the bumper injury. In the second phase, injuries occur on the side of the first impact, for example on the head and chest. In the third phase, the injury is on the opposite side, and all regions are injured by the blow against the ground. In the fourth phase, parallel abrasions corresponding to the sliding of the body along the ground appear. Attention: in phase 2 the injury is on the side of the impact, and in phase 3 on the opposite side.

t: Case analysis and quick question: young child pedestrian
n: Case analysis: a young child pedestrian. A young child pedestrian collided with the front of a moving car, and the speed of the car was low. In the child the primary impact falls on the region above the centre of gravity, so the second phase does not occur. At low speed the fourth phase may also be absent. In a bumper injury, the bones of the leg are broken with a passenger car and the femora with a lorry; the fracture is triangular, with its base on the side of the primary impact. Quick question: which phases are expected in this child, and what does the bumper injury show about the car?

t: Running over by a wheel: five phases
n: We consider the five phases of running over by a wheel. The first phase is impact: the wheel strikes the body. The second is displacement. The third is mounting: the wheel mounts the body. The fourth is dismounting: the wheel leaves the body. The fifth is secondary displacement of the body. In complete running over, the wheel passes across the body; in incomplete running over, it only mounts the body. The direction relative to the axis of the body may be transverse, oblique or longitudinal. Severe injuries are formed by compression of the body between the wheel and the ground; specific injuries occur mainly in phases 3-4.

We speak about tyre tread marks. A tread mark is a specific, that is, contact, injury; in running over by a wheel it is relatively common. The mark may take the form of an injury mark, that is, a bruise or abrasion, or of a deposit mark, that is, contamination. On the body there may be an injury mark or a deposit; on clothing mainly a deposit. A positive mark is formed by the raised part of the tread and gives an abrasion and a bruise. A negative mark is formed by the recessed part of the tread and gives only a bruise. Attention: positive and negative marks are not the same; their injury pictures differ.

We consider injuries by body region. Injuries in the third and fourth phases depend on which region of the body the wheel passed over. When the head is run over, multiple fractures of the skull and facial bones and crushing of the brain are seen; complete or partial separation of the auricles is also possible. In the chest the ribs are broken multiply on both sides. In the pelvis and leg, multiple fractures of the pelvis and comminuted fractures of the leg occur, and the organs of the pelvic cavity are injured. As a rule, the injury is more severe on the side from which the wheel mounted the body.

Case analysis: wheel mark. A contamination mark from a tread was found on the clothing, and abrasions and bruises on the body; running over is suspected. First question: what does the mark on the body look like? A positive mark is an abrasion with bruising, and a negative mark is a bruise only. Second question: how is the type of transport determined? The mark of a tractor tyre differs sharply from that of a car tyre, so the marks are compared. Third question: does the absence of injury in the fourth phase mean there was no running over? No: at a speed above 20 km/h the wheel bounces off.

t: Inside the car: injuries of the driver
n: We consider the injuries of the driver inside the car. In the driver, injuries are formed in 4 phases: first the legs strike the panel, then the chest strikes the steering wheel, then the head and neck strike the roof section and the glass, and finally the body is thrown backwards. On striking the steering wheel, a crescent-shaped abrasion and bruise form on the chest, and a contused wound on the chin. The injuries are located on the front and left surfaces. At high speed there may be a pedal mark on the sole of the shoe.

The question of passengers and the seat belt. In the front seat the head moves sharply forward, the skull and facial bones are broken, and the brain is contused. From windscreen fragments, abrasions and incised wounds occur on the face; at high speed the passenger may be thrown out. The front seat is the most dangerous because the body is not fixed. In the rear seat the danger is less, and the impact is against the back of the front seat. At the normal speed, the belt prevents injury; at high speed it becomes an injuring factor itself: a diagonal belt may cause injury to the cervical ligaments, rupture of the sternoclavicular joint and rib fractures.

t: Falling out of the car and a fall from a height
n: We compare falling out of a car and a fall from a height. In falling out there are three phases: impact against the parts of the vehicle, falling to the ground, and sliding along the ground. The main injury is formed on falling to the ground: on the head, fractures of the skull and cervical vertebrae, and on the legs, indirect fractures. At a speed above 25 km/h, injuries of the internal organs arise from concussion of the body. In falling out of a car there are marks of sliding along the ground, that is, parallel abrasions. In a fall from a height there is no third phase of sliding along the ground; the direct injury is formed on falling to the ground, and the indirect injury likewise.

t: Injuries in a fall by body part
n: We consider the injuries in a fall by body part. Most often the body lands on the ground head first: the skull and facial bones are broken, the brain is contused, and a fracture of the odontoid process of the second cervical vertebra is possible. In landing on the chest, the upper (1-4) and middle (5-8) ribs are injured; in landing on the buttocks, the pelvic bones and the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae, which is a compression fracture. Attention: in landing on the feet, the foot is broken directly, while the leg, thigh, pelvis and lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae are broken indirectly. Direct and indirect are not the same. At a speed above 25 km/h, in all variants of a fall the body is shaken and the internal organs are injured; the higher the speed, the more severe the injury.

We consider injury from compression. Compression is very rare; by the mechanism of impact and compression, injuries are inflicted in two phases. In the first phase there is an impact with an external part, and a contact injury, that is, an abrasion, is formed. In the second phase the body is compressed between objects. The seams and folds of clothing leave marks on the skin in the form of haemorrhages; this is called an ecchymotic contour. When the chest and abdomen are compressed, death from compressive asphyxia, that is, suffocation due to compression, is possible.

t: Case analysis: inside, falling out, compression
n: Case analysis. A passenger in a high-speed collision was thrown out through the windscreen, landed on the ground head first and slid along the ground. Analysis: falling out after injury inside the car is usually a combined auto trauma. In falling out there are three phases: impact, falling to the ground, and sliding along the ground. Parallel strip-like abrasions from sliding along the ground distinguish falling out from an ordinary fall from a height. Quick question 3: if the body is compressed between a car and a tree, what type of auto trauma is this and how many phases does it have? Answer: compression, two phases.

We turn to motorcycle trauma. It has five types: collision with a pedestrian, running over, a fall, collision with another object, and the combined type. Motorcycle trauma occurs mainly in late spring, summer and early autumn, that is, there is seasonality. Auto trauma is common, while motorcycle trauma is much less so. In auto trauma injury does not occur in every case, whereas in motorcycle trauma the driver and passenger are injured in all cases. In auto trauma sliding along the ground, that is, the 4th phase, is observed; in motorcycle trauma it is not. Characteristic marks are found on the surfaces of the leg and thigh.

We consider the injuries in motorcycle trauma. When a motorcycle collides with a pedestrian, the blow comes from the wheel, handlebar, lever and footrest; abrasions, bruises and contused-lacerated wounds are formed on the leg, pelvis and abdomen. Unlike a car, a motorcycle is not stable, so the driver and passenger may be injured in all cases. Characteristic injuries: an arc-shaped abrasion and a contused wound on the front and inner surfaces of the leg and thigh, and fractures of the bones of the leg, sometimes of the femur. Running over by a motorcycle wheel is rare; the injuries are similar to those from a car but lighter, because the mass is smaller.

t: Rail trauma: pressure tracks and sliding tracks
n: We consider rail trauma. It has six types: collision, running over, a fall, injury inside the transport, compression and combined trauma. The sequence of marks is as follows: the wheel flange touches the body, a T-shaped abrasion is formed, that is, the pinch sign, a pressure track appears, with sliding tracks at the edge, and the body may be divided in two. The T-shaped abrasion is on the region facing the gap between the rails, from which the wheel emerges. When the body is divided, the edges on the rail side are smooth, and on the wheel side coarsely toothed.

We consider tractor trauma. It has six types: collision, running over, injury in the cab, a fall, compression and combined trauma. It occurs mainly in rural areas; it may also be observed in industry, construction and municipal services. In a collision with a wheeled tractor the 2nd phase is not observed, the chest, abdomen and internal organs are injured, and the tread mark differs from that of a car. In a collision with a crawler tractor the 4th phase is absent, the injury is local, and there are no indirect injuries. The teeth of a crawler tractor catch the clothing and body and draw them underneath; the contamination mark corresponds to the track links of the chain.

t: Aviation trauma: types and injuring factors
n: Aviation trauma: types and injuring factors. Aviation trauma has four types: injury inside the aircraft, on leaving it, on striking the ground, and injury on the ground. The factors act simultaneously or successively; there are also the blast wave, thermal and toxic factors. The table shows the main factors and consequences. Dynamic overload leads to cerebral anaemia and loss of consciousness. The oncoming air stream causes detachment of facial tissue and barotrauma. Explosive decompression causes pulmonary and ear barotrauma, and altitude decompression causes gas bubbles in the blood vessels. Identification of the bodies, especially of crew members, is of great importance.

We consider the injuring factors in aviation trauma in detail. Many factors act simultaneously or successively: dynamic and impact overload, the air stream, decompression, explosion, and the thermal factor. At 800 km/h and above the air stream acts like a solid body: ruptures of the corners of the mouth and detachment of the soft tissues of the face are seen. Explosive decompression is observed when pressurisation is lost above 8 km, and altitude decompression at 19 km and above. Thermal action is greater in passengers, because the fuel tanks are located in the middle of the fuselage. The toxic factor: carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, vinyl chloride.

We consider the tasks of examination in aviation trauma. In most cases aviation trauma is an emergency and is thoroughly investigated by a group of various specialists in the established manner. Identification of persons from bodies and remains is of great importance, especially of crew members. On the body of the pilot, the position of the body parts at the time of injury, the state of health, the presence of toxic substances in the body and the cause of death are thoroughly examined. The experts also study the pilot's medical documents.

t: Case analysis and quick question: rail and aviation trauma
n: Case analysis on rail and aviation trauma. First case: on the clothing and body of a victim found on a railway there are particles of oil and coal, and a T-shaped abrasion on the skin. What trauma is this? Quick question: on which side is the T abrasion, that is, the pinch? Answer: on the side facing the wheel, towards the gap between the rails, in the region from which the wheel emerges. Second case: an aircraft crashed from a great height after loss of pressurisation; the dead have ruptured tympanic membranes and haemorrhage in the middle ear. What is the cause? Attention: explosive decompression, above 8 km, differs from altitude decompression, which occurs at 19 km and above and forms gas bubbles in the subcutaneous fat.

Let us sum up. Transport trauma is divided into automobile, motorcycle, bicycle, tractor, rail, aviation and water types; more than 90 per cent of examinations concern auto trauma. Auto trauma has six types: collision, running over by a wheel, injury inside the car, a fall, compression and the combined type. Each type has its own phases: four in a collision, five in running over by a wheel, and three in falling out of a car. Injuries are divided into four groups: specific, characteristic, non-characteristic and imitative. This is important for examination, and also for correct diagnosis and treatment.
